0c929c2e13da8b88e97b65d9f4ffa0af7a008455.en: The 1990s in Ukraine were a time of instability, material deprivation and complex relationships between parents and children. Against this backdrop unfolds the touching friendship between little Timofey, a sensitive boy who grew up without a father’s care, and Felix – his grandmother’s eccentric friend, a veteran of the war in Afghanistan. Felix suffers from post-traumatic stress and finds solace in music and alcohol. ‘Rock. Paper. Hand grenade’ is a raw, yet tender and heart-warming coming-of-age story about the first lessons in kindness and cruelty, teenage love, and the role of family and friends in the unstable environment of post-Soviet Ukraine. Irina Tsilik’s feature film debut is a moving coming-of-age drama set against the backdrop of the 1990s. (And of an inscrutable future that turned out to be harsher and darker.) Irina co-wrote the screenplay for *Stone. Paper. Grenade* with her husband Artem Chekh, author of the novel *Who Are You?*. Chekh is currently serving in the Ukrainian army. His book, which inspired the film, is a biography of a real-life figure of whom he has fond memories. The film’s wonderfully melancholic pace is down to the director’s masterful handling of sound and music. Every scene is carefully thought out and calibrated. Three different actors – Andriy Cherednyk, Vladyslav Balyuk and Volodymyr Hladkyi – take on the role of Tymofii at different ages. The role of his mother is played by the talented Anastasia Karpenko, known for her brilliant performance in the film *How Is Katya?*. Ukrainian director and journalist Iryna Tsilik made a name for herself with the documentary *The Earth Is Blue Like an Orange* (2020), which won the competition at Sundance in 2020; and was selected for the Berlinale, IDFA and more than 100 other international festivals.

This text is like an emotional map of deeply hidden, personal territories, for which we spend our whole lives waiting to meet someone with whom to share them. It explores the nuances of feelings and the inspiration drawn from living – things that cannot be seen or touched. For anyone who has a complex relationship with life, inspiration is a precious and hard-to-find drug. When you do find it, however, you become a composer who has found a piano on a desert island. My characters meet on a ‘desert island’ and, thanks to the magnificent Radena Vulkanova, Julian Vergov and Petar Antonov, and Mariy Rosen’s direction, I am currently standing in silence, listening to their music. And our shared island is no longer deserted.

Does everything around you seem gloomy and monotonous?

Are you fed up with having pointless conversations?

Here’s the solution to all your problems!

THE TELEVISION!!!

Just an arm’s length away!

With just one click of a button, your life will change, carefree days will reign, and your happiness is guaranteed! Right now, at the lowest possible price, you’ll have the chance to settle comfortably on the sofa and a smile will instantly light up your face!

Tune in to the most absurd evening, where the telly becomes the third member of the family, and reality and illusion collide with such force that the sofa springs will creak for a very long time.

This is a tragic farce in which laughter erupts where you least expect it, and the truth is so absurd that it sounds like fiction. Words fly like slaps, love drowns in adverts, and stars die on television – but always with a generous dose of glamour.

‘PRIVATE SCREENING’ is a show that won’t let you doze off on the sofa, but grabs you and throws you straight into the eye of the storm. Where the remote control is a weapon, the heart is the target, and chaos dictates the rules. It is here that laughter and tears intertwine in a frenzied dance, where tenderness collides head-on with hysteria, and love seems both madly funny and terribly tragic.

154e6b1728e8324d1a5a02a847a54a40ad86538f.en:
‘Art’ is a moving story about art, friendship and our ability to remain true to ourselves, but also to our friends, when we see the world in a different way.

How much would you pay for a white painting? Does it matter who the artist is? Can we call a painting ‘art’ if all we see before us is a white canvas?

Serge (Petar Petrov – Pero) buys a painting for an exorbitant sum. It consists of a large canvas, painted white, with ‘fine white diagonal stripes’. To one of his best friends – Mark (Georgi Gotzin) – the painting is ‘rubbish’ and Serge has lost his mind. Their mutual best friend, Ivan (Kiril Nedkov), finds himself in the awkward position of having to navigate between the two, even though he himself is bogged down in countless personal problems related to the preparations for his wedding.

Can a single painting put long-standing friendships to the test? The arguments ‘for’ and ‘against’ the painting cross the line of good taste. The three best friends use it as a pretext to say what they really think of one another, and their friendships seem increasingly fragile and a source of weariness rather than inspiration.

Will Serge, Mark and Ivan manage to preserve their 15-year friendship, or will a single painting bring it to an end?

With the arrival of the boy’s mother – a famous actress – and her friend – a great writer, who possess everything the young couple aspire to, everything changes in an instant. 17af1af29ab33fefaa5599be1b06a55f56e529d5.en:
The whisky’s flowing, the truths are coming to light, and the rain won’t stop.

What do you get when you put four women, a steam cleaner and a stolen idea together? Answer: total chaos and egos soaked to the bone!

‘Code Yellow’ is a comedy that asks the question: Can the women’s revolution happen without someone having to clean up afterwards?

Niki, a talented young architect on the verge of completing her first solo project, is getting ready for an important dinner with her boss. But instead, her neighbour Emma turns up at her door – armed with feminist slogans and the unsettling ability to turn any conversation into a lecture on patriarchy. Whilst Niki tries to get her to leave, her boss cancels the meeting on the pretext of having ‘stomach trouble’.

After three glasses of whisky and a host of conspiracy theories, Niki and Emma sneak into the architectural firm to look for ‘clues’. But they aren’t the only ones with this idea. There they find Adriana – the boss’s elegant wife – who is looking for a slightly different sort of compromising evidence against her husband!

As the rain falls harder and harder, flooding the basements, the tension in the office mounts, and the evening turns into a comical confrontation when the cleaner, Blagovesta, joins the group.

The four women turn out to be far more involved with the boss than they ever imagined.

And so, four women, each completely different from the other, armed with a bottle of whisky and a steam cleaner, embark on a night full of comical situations, in which, driven by their feminist rebellion, they organise a fun and chaotic plan for revenge.

Matteo meets Greta in Rome. He is playing tennis when she, on her way to her own wedding, stops for a set with him, a complete stranger. After thrashing him, she dashes off to get married with a beaming smile. Not only has he been defeated on the court, but Mateo is already in love – yet what can he do? Years later, in San Sebastián, their paths cross once more. Mateo is at a Bruce Springsteen concert when he spots Greta searching for her missing daughter. He then sees her again by chance in a Roman café. She is still with her husband, and Mateo has recently got married… Inspired by the stories of Eshkol Nevo, *It Will Happen Tonight* celebrates those moments when the universe seems to knock on the door with a wink, hinting at another possible life.

1fd7c61dfbde00c0f9b42db755b53c72afa4ca79.en:
‘Honour’ is a brutally honest play, written with a sharp pen, humour and elegance. It delicately yet boldly explores the trials a person goes through to discover the deepest meaning of the word ‘love’. What happens when the shared values and responsibilities in a perfectly harmonious marriage suddenly begin to fade? Honour and George have been married for 32 years. Both are acclaimed authors, although poetry has taken a back seat in Onor’s life to her devotion as a wife and mother. But when the opportunity arises to revitalise one’s life, at the expense of the happiness and security of others in the family, it is as if the whole world is turned upside down. Ivaylo Hristov sets the play at a brisk pace. On the stage, designed with minimalist yet striking effect, the four wonderful actors give their all. Events flow seamlessly into one another and escalate relentlessly. Until the finale arrives – perhaps a little breathless, but deeply lyrical.

The play is being staged for the first time in Bulgaria.

This silent observation gradually becomes an intimate journey – a tale of survival and love, loss and hostility. Confronted with the consequences of human actions, Helgestad raises a fundamental question: can empathy and understanding bridge the gap between humans and animals before it is too late? 2e976c1040b76950d0d8f6fc098313b724a57b30.en:
It might not sound realistic, but that’s only because you’ve never been stuck in… THE LIFT.

This is the story of two strangers forced to spend the night together in a broken-down lift, stuck between floors. She has to get home at all costs. He’s running late. And time is running out. Is it chance or a twist of fate that brings them together?

Four walls and two people create a new reality, demanding answers they are not ready to give.

What is the price of freedom? Are we afraid of the truth? Can we break free from the prejudices and rules that define us?

A dead-end situation becomes the only way out for two people who want to escape but cannot. How long can this illusion last? Will we hide from reality, or will the lift doors open and time continue its course?

‘The Lift’ is a play that offers no easy answers.

It confronts the characters – and the audience – with a choice: the security of the familiar or the risk of the unknown? Sometimes the way out lies not in the outside world, but in what changes within us.

The question that remains is not whether we will get out, but what we will be like when we do.

In a small university town, the artist Evelyn has won a commission to create a sculptural installation. At the Museum of Art, she meets Adam, a scruffy man in his thirties who juggles his work commitments as a security guard at the museum, a sales assistant at the university bookshop and his role as co-author of a book he is writing with his best friend, Philip. Adam’s relationship with Evelyn leads not only to his physical transformation, but also to a series of changes in his way of life. Adam’s transformation into a popular and attractive man does not go unnoticed by his closest friends, leading to unexpected changes in both his personal and social life. In his new self, the young man finds himself entangled in the subtle, almost invisible web of the dangerous transformation to which all forms of art lead.

Stefan Tsanev tells us about it… and about Ancient Greece, and about Bulgaria today, and perhaps about the world of tomorrow. Because he does not merely follow events, but manages to stay one step ahead of them! He speaks of power and democracy, of individual freedom, of the right to bear one’s own name. 398388964fbda7d451589cc221508857e7303d9d.en:
‘Ah, those ghosts!’ is one of Eduardo De Filippo’s most iconic and beloved comedies, in which the line between reality and illusion is as thin as smoke. The story takes us to a huge, empty Neapolitan palace, rumoured to be haunted by ghosts. Pasquale is a man with a noble heart, but plagued by poverty. He moves in as a tenant, hoping to turn it into a guesthouse. When inexplicable things begin to happen and ‘gifts’ from the afterlife start appearing in the house, Pasquale chooses to believe in miracles rather than the bitter truth. Because sometimes it is easier to believe in a ghost than to face the truth head-on.

A play about the human need to delude ourselves in order to survive. With plenty of smiles and the eternal question: which are the real ghosts – those that roam the rooms, or those we hide within our own souls?

3b2149543c2b9e5d46a4738e1c1be50382c4698f.en: At the Comédie-Française, preparations are in full swing for a production of *Macbeth*, Shakespeare’s famous tragedy. But just three hours before Nina’s directorial debut, complete chaos ensues – first the technical equipment fails, then the weaknesses and selfish outbursts of the actors in the troupe threaten to ruin the premiere. As the tension backstage mounts, Nina begins to see visions of Molière himself, who reproaches her for staging Shakespeare rather than one of his own plays. Caught between hallucination and reality, between attempts to calm the actors and her helpless baby, Nina resolves to keep the show going at any cost. Because the golden rule of the ‘Comédie-Française’ is never to cancel a performance. But does dedication always pay off? And is it possible for a play like *Macbeth*, whose central themes are betrayal and the corruption of power, to be interpreted as a comedy?

3d88f95ef631d1514efbc143ca29960bb068bda8.en: The story begins in Trigrad – the heart of the Rhodopes, where ancient legends, music and the mountains intertwine. It is here that the gaida reveals itself not merely as a musical instrument, but as a spiritual bridge between people, cultures and generations. The main character, Mitko, lost his younger brother, Yuli, several years earlier. In the final months of his life, the only thing that managed to lift Yuli from the burden of his illness was his desire to learn to play the gaida. After his death, Mitko follows in his footsteps – he takes up the bagpipes and embarks on a personal journey in memory of his brother, seeking meaning, solace and a bond that cannot be broken. The film follows this extraordinary journey, which connects Bulgaria and California through the power of music and brotherly love. From the Rhodopes, the story takes us to Los Angeles, where Mitko meets three extraordinary individuals – the bagpiper Eric Riegler, whose performances feature in the film *Braveheart*, the Bulgarian bagpiper Petro Dushkov; and the technological visionary and collector of musical instruments from around the world, Jaron Lanier. Each of these encounters reveals different possibilities of the gaida as a musical instrument and its extraordinary impact on people who, on the surface, inhabit completely different worlds. The journey concludes with a return to Bulgaria, to the village of Gela, where we meet the masters of the bagpipe who keep this centuries-old art alive. Thus, the film becomes a story of memory, hope and the power of music to connect people across time and distance.

4769be8d7ae26222e68a983a3eb0362fcd83ad85.en: Fifteen stab wounds in 27 seconds. This is what Salman Rushdie went through before opening his only functioning eye and looking at the camera. Together with his wife, Rachel Eliza Griffiths, the writer decided to document his slow return to life a few days after the brutal attack in New York. Oscar-winning director Alex Gibney unfolds a painful and deeply insightful story that traces Salman Rushdie’s rehabilitation and pays tribute to his indomitable spirit, humour and optimism. The story begins following the publication of *The Satanic Verses*, when a religious edict, a ‘fatwa’, was issued against Rushdie by the Iranian Ayatollah Khomeini. From that moment on, the writer lived under constant threat for decades, fighting for the right to free public expression. The culmination of the persecution is captured in a harrowing recording of the assassination attempt… Rushdie will return to the scene of the crime to bring this dark chapter of his life to a close, but is that even possible? A powerfully resonant documentary narrative that explores the themes of religion and art as an explosive combination. Salman Rushdie, a brilliant writer and intellectual with a cosmopolitan spirit, reflects on violence, forgiveness and the right to free speech – themes that are more relevant than ever.

47837d59e5b2585b7b1019f8b78b6e18d111e0eb.en: Nora, Thomas and their daughter Ida live peacefully on a secluded farm. Their only neighbour is the Italian artist Cristina (Monica Bellucci). Whilst everyone is preparing for a surprise party to celebrate Nora’s birthday, three suspicious men begin loitering around the house. Before long, they take it upon themselves to join the celebrations. Tranquillity gives way to anxiety and tension. The film is an adaptation of the noir novel of the same name by Laurent Mouvignier – a skilfully layered socio-psychological narrative structured as a crime thriller. The author puts forward the idea that dangers and anxieties do not strike suddenly, but slowly seep into everyday life. As the characters’ pasts come to light, it turns out that almost every one of them bears the burden of some form of remorse, fear, past humiliation or unresolved trauma. Laurent Mouvignier is one of the most highly regarded contemporary authors in France and has recently cemented his status as a brilliant novelist by winning the prestigious Goncourt Prize for his monumental novel *The Empty House*. The film is not recommended for children under 16.

One day, her grandmother fainted whilst watering the flowers at the local cemetery. Ida panics, but suddenly hears a mysterious, angelic song. Her grandmother miraculously recovers, and the girl is amazed by the power of the song. Convinced that singing could save her grandmother’s life, Ida decides to join the school choir, even though she cannot sing. After the audition, she is rejected, but a shy girl named Terezka will try to help her. Through the lens of childhood loneliness, I wanted to explore the space between the lightness of everyday life and the quiet presence of inevitable loss. Faced with this feeling, children seek refuge in their imagination, in play, in solitude or in moments shared with friends, and find security wherever they can. The film unfolds precisely in these fleeting moments, in which innocence and vulnerability coexist. Esther Ivačić

70ec406701d789f4143a425b5ee82a0cfd46aaba.en: This is a play that pokes fun at clichés – the clichés of love at first sight, and indeed at second and third sight. It also pokes fun at marriage rituals, whether held in civil registry offices or in church. And at the reasons for getting married, too. A good-natured mockery of traditional family values, as well as of generally accepted human norms, takes centre stage. The performance pokes fun at homophobia, but also at its cause – homosexuality. It has the audacity to mock violence. Why? To render it powerless. It reminds us that senseless cruelty has, in fact, no reason and ought not to exist. All these things are justified by a sort of ‘Americanisation’ of humanity. In our case, a strong dose of ‘Balkanisation’ accompanies this Americanisation. Can we laugh at cruelty and primitiveness? Yes! We’ll survive simply because we’ll laugh. I know from experience that a smile disarms. My desire, and that of the performers, is for the violence in the production to have a certain ‘Tarantino-esque’ flavour, combined with a dose of ‘Marx Brothers’-style comedy. We also ask the question: where is the world heading, and how far has it gone… ‘Where on earth are we heading?’, as Radičkov would say. I would say ‘through the rye’, so that I might finally pose the ‘clever’ closing question: is there a Saviour in the rye? You’ll have to see for yourselves. Come and see us! Let’s hope the end of the show doesn’t coincide with the end of our world, ha ha ha!

82f1aef11401bd4c8326782cf921d0b65eb5c7f3.en: The film focuses on the lives of Jean and Corinne Lucher – a father and daughter in occupied France. She is a young film star, whilst he is a powerful media magnate and a friend of Otto Abetz, the influential Nazi ambassador in Paris. The story is told from the perspective of Corinne, once hailed as ‘the new Garbo’. As she records her thoughts on a borrowed tape recorder, she tries to reconcile her unwavering love for her father with the fact that he was executed for treason in 1946. Despite its impressive running time of over three hours, *Lights and Shadows* attracted more than 300,000 cinema-goers in France in the first week after its release alone. The film also sparked a heated debate regarding the Vichy regime. Whilst many critics from the centre and the right praised it as a masterpiece that captures the historical nuances, left-wing publications such as L’Humanité have criticised it for downplaying the actions of those who voluntarily served the Nazi killing machine right to the very end. Laurent Joly – a leading French historian specialising in the Vichy regime and state anti-Semitism – has praised the film for its ‘ambiguity’ and ‘duplicity’. According to Joly, “it was not pacifism that drove Luchère towards collaboration, but his venality and lack of morals”. ‘Light and Shadow’ is a harrowing reflection on moral compromises, cruelty, valour and all that remains in our lives against the backdrop of major historical upheavals. Rather than overwhelming the viewer with raw emotion, Xavier Giannoli unfolds the story with patience and delicacy. Silence is part of the narrative language, whilst the contrast between light and shadow serves as a subtle metaphor for memory, absence and the fragile resilience of human bonds. The cinematography in *Rays and Shadows* is never an end in itself or merely decorative – it serves the film’s emotional core. The actors’ performances are restrained and precise, devoid of theatricality. Every gesture feels authentic and dramaturgically justified. If you’re looking for a conventional plot or instant gratification, this isn’t the film for you. But if you’re ready for something more contemplative and introspective – something that resonates rather than forcing its message upon you – *Rays and Shadows* will offer you an exceptionally rewarding experience. A film of rare sensitivity, in which the invisible is just as important as the visible. (anonymous viewer review)

8640a28c964a2f31063177d8affefccc1679af6c.en:
‘Stories’ is a play by one of the most interesting contemporary British playwrights – Nina Raine – which has never before been staged in Bulgaria. Set within the genre of contemporary tragicomedy, the play explores an important issue for modern Europeans – the problem of reproduction – not only in its biological sense, but primarily in its socio-existential context. Is the individual truly disappearing? And why does the grand narrative of one’s life fragment into a multitude of smaller ones?

At the centre of the action is Anna – a woman in her late thirties who dreams of becoming a mother. After her long-term relationship breaks down and her hopes of a traditional family are shaken, she decides to take her fate into her own hands and find a way to have a child without a permanent partner. Thus begins a series of unusual, comical and sometimes painful encounters with various men, which reveal not only the contradictions in modern relationships, but also societal attitudes towards women, the biological clock and the right to personal choice.

Anna is a casting director who is conducting the most important auditions of her life – in search of a father for her future baby. And so the story of her personal film turns out to be a quest for its own plot and meaning. ‘Stories’ is also a play about all the narratives that modern people invent to save themselves from loneliness and a lack of meaning.

But can their relationship survive the cold light of day? The film tells the story of a woman experiencing her first love, but alongside the beauty of romance, it also explores the contradictions, paradoxes and deceptions inherent in human nature. A timeless love story, born of the imagination of Miéko Kawakami, author of the novels *Sky* and *Breasts and Eggs*. 913476c9a86002306dff9ab4d974555a7ec51196.en: ‘Sing well, live well, die well’ – this is the motto that the opera prima donna Carlotta Berlumy has followed throughout her life and career. And it seems she has truly managed to live up to it: blessed with a naturally beautiful voice, she won a competition at the age of 17, and by the age of twenty she was already singing in *Aida* at La Scala in Milan. Life has been generous to her – showering her with talent, loyal admirers and numerous lovers. But the emergence of another opera star seemed to cast a shadow over her triumphant march across the opera stages – Maria Callas. When she first met her, Carlotta failed to recognise the threat posed by the ambitious Greek woman. Later, however, she began to see the malevolent influence of Callas in every professional and romantic setback she suffered. Her rival is her complete opposite: with a voice like a ‘fire-engine siren’, her innovative stage presence, and her model-like appearance. But the most inexplicable thing is the behaviour of the audience – the spectators admire Carlotta, but some prefer to watch Callas and boo her, rather than listen to Berlumy. Callas’s failure arouses greater interest than Berlumi’s triumph. What is the key to this mystery? What is the magic with which Callas manages to captivate crowds all over the world? Carlotta Berlumi seeks to answer these questions in the twilight of her days, when all that remains for her is to fulfil the final part of her motto – ‘a good death’.

917a0d468dddec2fcf16d4b38a325baa8c65f6cb.en:
Valeri Petrov transforms Dumas’s classic plot into a ‘playground’ for words, rhymes and stunts.

Everything on stage happens ‘as if by chance’, yet with complete sincerity. We return to the pure form of theatrical play, in which horses exist only in the actors’ imagination, and the enemy is merely a figment of the imagination.

It all comes down to just how far the actors’ inventiveness can take them.

Our musketeers are not unattainable superheroes, but entirely ordinary people – vulnerable, sensitive, very witty, and sometimes a little naïve. They are not preoccupied with existential questions, and nothing human is alien to them.

‘One for all, all for one’ is not an empty phrase, but the bond between four distinct and unique characters who, were they not so, would not have stood the test of time for a century and a half.

An exploration of the concept of ‘honour’ in a world full of intrigue (but presented lightly and without moralising).

Good always finds a way to triumph, even through a smile.

Why should I waste an hour of my life watching

‘Honourable Musketeer’ by Valeri Petrov?

Because it offers entertainment for all ages.

Because it restores the joy of pure, unadulterated theatrical action.

Because it teaches us not to take ourselves too seriously.

‘The Honest Musketeer’ is a celebration of the imagination, in which the most powerful weapon is not the sword, but a witty remark!

980b5a6ad11aa65f3b23404288d053153d47b72d.en:
‘The Minister’s Wife’ was written by Branislav Nušić in 1931, in the midst of the Great Depression. A context from which the Balkans, for a host of historical, cultural and geopolitical reasons, seem as though they will never escape. It’s always a crisis, there’s never enough, we’re always screwed and bitter. At least we’re not ugly. And we’re hardly dirty. Or so we think. And we’re always dreaming that, God willing, we’ll lead our father’s brigade and sort out the country. And in ‘no time at all’. What other nations, under different circumstances, have achieved over a century, we do in a ‘five-year plan’. And we end up like a dog in a field. Just like that. A complete shambles.

Our heroine, the Minister’s Wife, wakes up one day as if in a dream, her knickers still in tatters, and whilst she’s wondering how to make ends meet, the irony of chance spits her out into the ministerial backwaters. And so the same old story about the ladder begins…

‘BLACK COMEDY’? It probably sounds familiar to you, doesn’t it? Yes, even if you haven’t seen Peter Shaffer’s play, you’ve certainly heard of it. And now you have the chance to see it on stage at the “BULGARIAN ARMY” Theatre.

“BLACK COMEDY” is regarded as one of the funniest comedies written in the second half of the 20th century. Right from its premiere at the National Theatre in London in 1965, the production became a real hit and soon won over audiences all over the world.

‘BLACK COMEDY’ is a madcap farce that unfolds… in the DARK. Yes, it is indeed the DARK that plays the leading role in this comedy. But what happens when DARKNESS is LIGHT, and light turns to darkness? The logical question, ‘What is a person capable of when they know that nobody can see them?’ lies at the heart of the mechanism that, throughout the entire performance, provokes laughter in ‘BLACK COMEDY’ at the ‘BULGARIAN ARMY’ Theatre.

b78cfcec5d858d86d2920f7817cacea025315a92.en:
A curious little girl is hiding in the crown of a large tree. Beneath it, a white-bearded, good-natured old man, on his way to the sea, sits down to rest. He spots the little girl in the branches and decides to cheer her up with a magic trick. And who doesn’t love magic tricks and sorcery? We’re all captivated by them, aren’t we? Perhaps because it’s delightfully astonishing when the impossible seems easy and entirely achievable. When an object vanishes or appears before our eyes in an instant, having come or vanished into thin air – a playing card, a bouquet, a rabbit or even a violin… We probably love these tricks because they suggest that the world and life hold all manner of magic, that friendship, hope and joy are always possible, that every moment can surprise us with its magic, as long as we do not hide too stubbornly amongst the branches of our own tree.

The play is being staged for the first time in Bulgaria.

“#antitaga” is a theatre performance based on texts by the poet and playwright Stefan Ivanov. ‘#antituga’ portrays the inner world of the modern individual, deprived of successful social interactions, their absurd and dark humour, but also their powerlessness within the society and state in which they live, and their constant self-reproach for their inability to adapt to these circumstances and build their own happiness.

‘#antitaga’ is about a person searching for meaning and a way out of the labyrinth into which they have led themselves, guided by their belief that perhaps love is enough. ‘#antituga’ is about suicidal thoughts and behaviour, clinical depression, everyday ‘burnout’, psychological trauma, addictions, bad habits, a broken society, standing up for one’s civic convictions, a lack of empathy, unrequited love, chronic negativity, laughter and death. These are themes that are becoming increasingly relevant in times of war, epidemics, economic crises and social fragmentation.

‘#antisadness’ raises the question of whether and how to carry on living, whilst waging war with oneself and in search of inner and outer peace.

bbe15fd1c1ad3bcc9b3429c4d7aabad952f13e29.en:
‘HERCULES VS AUGYAS’ is a modern interpretation of the classical myth of Hercules, centred on his fifth labour, known as the cleaning of the Augean stables.

Our version, however, transports the mythological hero into the world of modern politics, absurd bureaucracy and moral social decay, and confronts him with a challenge that even for Hercules begins to seem insurmountable. He comes up against an impenetrable wall of apathy, conformism and stupidity, and gradually begins to realise that physical strength alone will get him nowhere. The play is permeated with irony, sarcasm and humour, which depict not so much the filth itself as people’s willingness to live amidst it and the absence of any moral ideal. For me, as a director, this was precisely the great provocation of this text – the question: ‘Who is today’s Hercules?’. Our Hercules turned out to be not so much a mythical hero as an ordinary person who can be great through the choices they make.

‘HERCULES VS AUGYAS’ is a production with a sharp sense of humour and an attempt to hold up a mirror to ourselves and the audience – a funny yet painfully topical piece that reminds us that the country we live in actually depends solely on us, and if we want change, then we must start with ourselves first.”

This conflict forms the basis of *Inter Alia* – one of the most interesting new plays of the last few years. In a style that blends humorous stand-up comedy with a courtroom-family thriller, *Inter Alia* explores the relativity of consent in heterosexual relationships, the fragility of contemporary ideologies and the difficult balance between career and family faced by the modern individual.

How did a farmer’s son build a multi-billion-dollar luxury empire? Brunello Cucinelli is the founder of the renowned Italian fashion house specialising in luxury cashmere garments. Through documentary footage, personal recollections and dramatised scenes, the film traces his journey from his childhood in Umbria to international success, revealing his philosophy of ‘humanistic capitalism’, which is founded on human dignity, artistic mastery and social responsibility. Tornatore builds the narrative around a symbolic card game between Cuccinelli and an enigmatic opponent, who remains unidentified until the very end. Thus, the story becomes a parable about fate, time and the courage to follow one’s dreams, whilst Nicola Piovani’s music lends the film an added sense of poetry. Unconventional in form, ‘Brunello: The Visionary Gentleman’ is a true cinematic treat and yet further proof that the director of ‘Cinema Paradiso’ and *The Legend of the Pianist* is an unrivalled master of dramatic vision and epic scope in cinema.

In 1939, on the eve of the Second World War, Swedish swimmer Sally Bauer defied social norms and expectations to achieve her goal. She was determined to become the first Scandinavian woman to swim across the English Channel. The film raises questions about motherhood and ambition, personal choice and the price of freedom. When she realised that she was a real person, she began to research her life and discovered a book containing Bauer’s reflections on the year leading up to her swim across the English Channel.

Three women shut away in their little house near the gloomy Irish Sea. Time and again – as if in an endless game – they relive a long-gone night in the town’s dance hall. A night that seems to have become their only reality. The reality of impossible love.

This ritual is interrupted only by the unexpected appearances of an utterly absurd delivery man, who bursts into the ladies’ kitchen to bring them fish. And to recount the latest gossip circulating around the island. At first glance, his comical presence distracts the characters from their bitter memories.

But is that all there is to it? Is it possible, after all, for love to find its way to this house, so far removed from the dance hall?

‘The New Dance Hall’ marks the dazzling Bulgarian stage debut of the renowned contemporary Irish playwright Enda Walsh. The play masterfully combines explosive humour, verging on the grotesque, with unexpectedly lyrical imagery and an almost poetic language. The author constructs a new theatrical form of the theatre of the absurd, through which he specifically attacks the painful triviality of our times.

The play is being staged for the first time in Bulgaria.

The film is a loose adaptation of the documentary book of letters *When Life Suddenly Takes a Turn*, co-written by Maoko Miyano and Maho Isono. The book bears witness to their warm friendship and mutual support. Ryusuke Hamaguchi transports this tender, intellectually stimulating and humane story to the Parisian suburbs. With his first film made outside Japan, the director demonstrates his unique gift for employing subtle emotional nuances and balancing dialogue with silence. The plot unfolds patiently, with an exceptional sensitivity to every gesture, allowing the conversations and silences to generate profound emotional power.

ec0454dcc1d5cfdcc5a46f4f874af8192e575b72.en: Young Violette Tréne is the caretaker of the cemetery in a small town in Burgundy. A job that many would find off-putting, but for her compassionate heart it is a salvation and a refuge. In this oasis of silence, free from the hustle and bustle of everyday life, Violette has developed a knack for savouring the little things: tending to the flowers, a fragrant cup of tea, freshly picked fruit. Her tranquillity is disrupted by the sudden appearance of a mysterious man who attempts to unearth long-buried secrets. In turn, Violet is forced to confront her past in order to give life and love a new chance. Director Jean-Pierre Jeunet, winner of dozens of awards and honours for iconic films such as *The Unbelievable Fate of Amélie Poulain* (a César for Best Film and Best Director, a BAFTA for Best Screenplay, an Oscar nomination, and more), *The Longest Engagement*, ‘Delicacy’ and ‘The City of Lost Children’, returns with a new cinematic gem, a life-affirming tale and a feast for the senses – an apotheosis of humanity, delicacy and beauty. The film is a masterful adaptation of the international bestseller *Water for the Flowers* by Valérie Perrin, translated into over 30 languages and selling more than a million copies worldwide. The book has won numerous awards, including the prestigious ‘Maison de la Presse’ prize. ‘Water for the Flowers’ was also the best-selling book in Italy in 2020.

ec924723d56c437e112c03b027f817f76f981814.en: An insightful portrait of the American novelist and essayist Siri Hustvedt: her literary evolution, her relationship with Paul Auster, and her reflections on feminism and the philosophy of our times. Rather than following the logic of a chronological biography, the film explores the ideas and personal experiences that have shaped Hustvedt’s views and underpin her work. The film traces Siri Hustvedt’s life from her childhood in Minnesota to her move to New York, where she became one of the leading voices in contemporary American literature. Her reflections on literature, identity, memory, neuroscience, psychoanalysis, feminism and the creative process are interwoven with scenes from her daily life and landmark interviews. A central theme of the film is her long-standing partnership with the irreplaceable American writer Paul Auster. Whilst filming was underway – a process that lasted several years – Auster received a serious diagnosis. Thus, the film, which begins as a portrait of a writer’s intellectual life, gradually evolves into an intimate and moving reflection on love, illness, vulnerability and grief. Many critics note that this emotional shift lends the film’s narrative a powerful resonance and depth. The title is metaphorical. It suggests that the ‘self’ cannot be clearly captured or defined. One approaches it indirectly – through memory, language, relationships, art and the body. This image is largely consistent with Hustvet’s work, which repeatedly questions the stability of identity and emphasises that consciousness is fluid and relative.

f18d5153902340b07e5739f1dffd937cbdf7dbe6.en: 1943. In the heart of the jungle, in a Japanese prisoner-of-war camp situated along the Thailand – Burma, Lieutenant-Colonel Dorigo Evans is tormented by the memory of a far too brief but fateful love affair – the one with his uncle’s wife, Amy Mulvaney. It is precisely this memory that becomes his inner anchor as he struggles to cling to life amidst the endless shadow of death. The love between Dorigo and Amy blossomed years earlier – from the moment they first met, she never left his thoughts, despite his long-standing marriage to Ella Evans, his secret affair with Lynette Maison and his life-changing friendship with the soldier Frank Gardner. An adaptation of the novel of the same name by Richard Flanagan, winner of the Man Booker Prize, ‘The Narrow Road to the Deep North’ is a multi-layered narrative: a timeless love story, an intimate exploration of character, a clash of cultures seen from both sides of the conflict, and an honest look at a long-standing partnership. The series *The Narrow Road to the Deep North* is produced by the Australian company Curio Pictures, with the support of Sony Pictures Television. Sean Grant is the screenwriter and executive producer, whilst Justin Kurzel is the director and also an executive producer. The screenplay adaptation is the result of a collaboration between screenwriter Sean Grant and Richard Flanagan himself.

f8225550bd66971942bf1ee693bdb7b41aebabc7.en: Marion Cotillard plays Edie, a film star whose fame is on the wane. The story is set in 1982. On the brink of a severe mental breakdown, Edie sets off for Rome to shoot a science-fiction film. She is accompanied by her make-up artist – the outspoken and open-minded Valentina (Noémie Merlan). Once the euphoria of arriving in the Eternal City has faded, Eddie is invited to appear on an eccentric talk show, where a man wearing a monkey mask hurls insults… Bernard Mandico has created a frenetic, irreverent and utterly unpredictable film – a sardonic provocation directed at the futile film industry. Its abrasive structure will either captivate you or shock and repel you, but one thing is certain – it will not leave you indifferent.

The film captures this unforgettable day through performances by Ozzy, Black Sabbath and some of the most influential names in rock music, as well as through the personal memories and reflections of the star musicians who were inspired by them. Viewers will also see exclusive behind-the-scenes footage revealing how the day itself unfolded. This is a historic and intimate farewell to Ozzy and to the band that changed music forever.

fbec30b0ba7f363fde68194a9a059b52577277ed.en: A young warrior, raised by the tribe that once slaughtered his own family, lives in ignorance of his past, surrounded by his enemies. When he uncovers the horrifying secret of his origins, he is forced to confront painful memories, betrayals and the brutal world in which he grew up. Torn between a thirst for revenge and the hope of redemption, he must choose whether to follow the path of blood or to break the cycle of violence. The *Kalevala* is a 19th-century epic compiled by Elias Lönnrot. It is regarded as Finland’s national epic and one of the most significant works in Finnish literature. The *Kalevala* has played a vital role in the development of Finnish national identity and in the consolidation of the Finnish language and national consciousness. An epic work of Scandinavian mythology, translated into 61 languages. It is Finland’s most widely translated literary work.
